name: Profile analysis (Ricketts E-line)

card.summary: A line from nose tip to chin used to judge how far the lips sit from the profile; a standard orthodontic reference, with preferences that vary by observer.
card.aka: E-line, esthetic line, esthetic plane, Gonzalez-Ulloa
card.note: Norms are population averages; studies show esthetic preferences differ across observer groups.

quick.overview:
The Ricketts esthetic line, or E-line, is drawn from the tip of the soft-tissue nose to the soft-tissue chin (pogonion) on a side-view image. Orthodontists use the distance from the lips to this line to describe how full or retrusive the profile is.

It is one of several profile analyses, and looksmaxxing discussions of chin and lip position borrow it as a way to describe the relationship between nose, lips and chin.
quick.mechanism: On a lateral cephalogram or profile photograph the line is drawn and the lower lip is measured against it. Wikipedia lists a published mean for lower lip to E-line of minus 2 mm with a standard deviation of 2 mm.
quick.risks: This is a measurement convention rather than a treatment. Cephalometric measurements are two-dimensional, and studies show that preferred profiles differ among observers of different backgrounds.

lead: The Ricketts E-line, also called the esthetic line or esthetic plane, is a straight line drawn on a side-view photograph or radiograph from the tip of the nose to the soft-tissue pogonion, the most forward point of the chin's soft tissue. The distance of the lips from this line is used to judge whether the lips sit in a balanced position between the nose and chin [1]. For people working on their profile, it provides a concrete way to see how the nose, lips and chin relate, which informs decisions about orthodontics, chin or nose work, lip fillers and jaw surgery.

The standard measurement is the lower lip to E-line distance (Li-EL), reported in the cephalometric literature as about minus 2 mm with a standard deviation of 2 mm, meaning the lower lip typically sits slightly behind the line [1]. Orthodontists and maxillofacial surgeons use the line when planning treatment, tracking change and checking whether goals were met [1][2]. Studies of profile change after orthodontic treatment and jaw surgery report lip position relative to esthetic lines [3][4][2].

The line comes from the orthodontic work of Robert M. Ricketts (1920-2003), whose cephalometric analysis compares a patient with norms adjusted for age, sex and race, and who argued that treatment should consider the face as a whole [8]. Esthetic preferences for lip position vary between observer groups and individuals, so published work treats Li-EL as a reference point and not as a single target [5][6]. In looksmaxxing forums, profile analysis threads discuss chin and lip projection together with nasal angles, with the E-line mentioned as one of several lines and ratios [7].

paras: Cephalometric analysis uses standardised side-view radiographs or photographs to measure the face. The E-line extends from the tip of the soft-tissue nose to soft-tissue pogonion; Li-EL is the distance of the lower lip from it. Wikipedia gives a norm of minus 2 mm with a standard deviation of plus or minus 2 mm for the lower lip and lists no upper-lip norm [1].

Because the line runs from the nose to the chin, changes to either structure move the line and change measured lip position: a more projecting nose or chin shifts the line forward and makes the lips appear more retrusive, and a smaller nose or chin does the opposite. Clinicians therefore read lip position together with nose and chin form [1][2].

Cephalometrics became practical after Holly Broadbent Sr. introduced the cephalostat, a head-holding device, in 1931, allowing standardised radiographs. Later analyses include the Downs and Steiner systems; Steiner published his in 1953 [1]. Robert M. Ricketts (1920-2003), an American orthodontist who trained under Allan Brodie, developed the Ricketts cephalometric analysis within his work on orthodontics, beginning in the 1950s; he published papers in 1960 based on cephalometric radiographs of about 1,000 patients [8][1].

Ricketts' Bioprogressive philosophy treats the face as a whole, not just the teeth and bite, and includes the Visual Treatment Objective, a planning tool in which an expected result is drawn on a tracing [8].

Ricketts was born on 5 May 1920 in Kokomo, Indiana, earned his dental degree at Indiana University in 1945, served as a US Navy dentist, and completed a master's in orthodontics at the University of Illinois under Allan G. Brodie in 1947 [8]. In the 1950s he promoted routine clinical use of cephalometric X-rays, in contrast to Brodie's and Broadbent's research emphasis on longitudinal growth, and reported his experience with 1,000 patients in 1960 [8]. His other best-known contributions include the .018-inch bracket slot (1970), treatment forecasting, and computerised cephalometrics; he founded the American Institute for Bioprogressive Education in 1981, wrote more than 30 books, and died in Scottsdale, Arizona in 2003 [8].

The E-line is one of several soft-tissue references. The Steiner S-line, from Cecil Steiner's 1953 analysis, runs from soft-tissue pogonion to the midpoint of the curve under the nose, and the guideline is that both lips ideally touch it, a qualitative target rather than a numeric norm [1]. Burstone's 1978 COGS analysis was developed for orthognathic surgery planning, and an Arnett soft-tissue analysis is also used in surgical planning [1]. Because each line uses different landmarks, the same profile can read as protrusive on one and balanced on another, which is why clinicians often cite more than one [1].

Plastic-surgery references add angles that looksmaxxing posters also use. Rhinoplasty texts give the nasofrontal angle as about 115 to 130 degrees (more acute in men), the nasofacial angle about 30 to 40 degrees, and the nasolabial angle about 90 to 95 degrees in men and 100 to 105 degrees in women, and describe tip-projection ratios such as the Goode method (about 0.55 to 0.60 of nasal length) [11].

sections.h: How nose, chin and lips change the reading
paras: Since the E-line is anchored at the nose tip and the chin, procedures that change either one move the reference. Chin augmentation (genioplasty) adds forward projection or adjusts height using implants or bone repositioning, and is often performed with rhinoplasty so that the profile looks balanced; techniques such as the T-osteotomy typically alter the chin by about 2 to 3 mm and can advance it [12]. Common effects include swelling, bruising and temporary lower-lip numbness, with infection, implant shifting or nerve injury less common [12].

Rhinoplasty can reduce a dorsal hump or alter the nasolabial angle, changing how the nose sits in profile [11]. Orthodontic tooth movement, functional appliances, jaw surgery and lip fillers change lip position relative to the line, which is why clinical papers report E-line change as an outcome [2][3][4]. Anyone considering a procedure is directed in the literature to surgeon and orthodontist assessment, because treatment planning also weighs bite, airway and skeletal factors [1][8].

Profile analysis threads on looksmax.org show users posting side photographs and measuring angles and chin position, often by ethnic group [7]. One widely read thread on African profiles argues that a chin level with the lower lip, common in some populations, reflects different dental-facial growth, nasal angles and convexity and should not be read as recessed on a Caucasian standard [7]. Orthodontic research likewise reports that the norms underlying the Ricketts analysis are adjusted by age, sex and race, and that judges of different backgrounds prefer different lip positions [8][5].

The vocabulary used in these threads (recessed chin, projection, convexity, prognathism, nose-chin relationship) overlaps with the cephalometric literature, but forum measurements are made on photographs, and cephalometric sources note that image magnification and head posture affect readings [1].

Dentists, orthodontists and oral and maxillofacial surgeons use cephalometric analysis to assess facial growth, plan treatment, monitor progress and confirm goals after treatment [1]. Soft-tissue measures such as the E-line are used to evaluate lip position after tooth movement, functional appliances and jaw surgery [3][4][2].
Lip fillers also change lip projection relative to the nose and chin, and the same reference lines are used to describe their effect on the profile.

Esthetic preference for lip position is not uniform. One study used four panels of 30 lay judges, European American, Hispanic American, Japanese and African, to view silhouette profiles of European American, Japanese and African American Class I and Class II orthodontic patients and examined whether judge and patient sex and race or ethnicity affect preferences for lip positions [5]. Another study compared photographs with silhouettes for evaluating African American profile esthetics [6].

A study of 30 attractive and 32 non-attractive subjects compared skeletofacial morphology from lateral head films to test whether facial beauty relates to specific jaw relationships, profile convexity and lip position [9].

Cephalometric images are two-dimensional projections of three-dimensional structures, and magnification and distortion can affect the detail visible [1]. Lip posture, head position and smile or rest posture alter a photograph's reading. A 2022 study evaluated fully automated cephalometric measurements from an AI platform [10].

Orthodontic extraction cohorts. A study of 160 patients aged 10 to 30 who had four first premolars removed examined soft-tissue profile changes across five sources of treated patients, including Tweed Foundation and Begg-technique records [3]. A later study also examined soft-tissue profile change after four-premolar extraction [4].

Functional appliances. A 2025 randomized trial in Scientific Reports enrolled 52 pubertal patients with skeletal Class II malocclusion, randomised to aesthetic or conventional Twin Block (26 each). The conventional group showed significant upper and lower lip retraction relative to Ricketts' E-line while the aesthetic group did not, with no significant difference between groups [2].

Jaw surgery. A 2026 retrospective study of 258 adults with skeletal Class III treated with mandibular setback surgery (vertical ramus osteotomy, genioplasty, or both) reported that E-line-based esthetic outcomes were achieved in about 47 to 50 percent of patients across groups [2].

Maxillary protraction. A 2026 study of 17 adolescents with skeletal Class III and maxillary deficiency treated with miniscrew-anchored protraction reported increased lip position and decreased nasolabial angle and facial convexity [2].
Perception studies. The rater-based studies above examined lay-judge preferences and attractiveness comparisons; they are observational and not interventional trials of the line itself [5][6][9].

lore.intro: Profile analysis threads on looksmax.org discuss chin projection and lip balance, often by ethnic group, and the esthetic line appears among several profile references [7].

claims.claim: Many African profiles look 'recessed' because the chin sits in line with the lower lip
claims.believers: A forum poster argues that many people see chin-in-line profiles as recessed, a perception he attributes to different dental-facial growth, nasal angles and convexity, and says this reflects a Caucasian reference standard [7].
claims.experts: Studies have examined whether judge and patient race and ethnicity affect preferred lip positions, using silhouette profiles of European American, Japanese and African American patients, and have compared photos with silhouettes for African American profile esthetics [5][6].

claims.claim: Ideal lips sit a set distance behind the E-line
claims.believers: Profile guides cite the Ricketts norm as an ideal for lip position.
claims.experts: The reported norm is minus 2 mm with an SD of 2 mm [1], and studies show preferences differ across observer groups [5].

claims.claim: A good profile requires lips in a fixed position relative to the E-line
claims.believers: Profile guides on forums cite the Ricketts figure as an ideal for lip position when discussing chin and lip balance.
claims.experts: Ricketts' analysis compares patients with norms adjusted for age, sex and race, and observer panels of different backgrounds prefer different lip positions [8][5].

claims.claim: Chin and nose changes can rebalance the whole profile
claims.believers: Posters discuss chin projection and nasal angles as the levers that determine how the profile reads [7].
claims.experts: Surgical references describe genioplasty and rhinoplasty as altering profile proportions, often performed together, with swelling, numbness and implant or nerve complications reported [12][11].

claims.claim: Photo-based line measurements are as reliable as clinical tracings
claims.believers: Forum users measure angles from side photographs and compare them with published ranges [7].
claims.experts: Cephalometric images are two-dimensional with magnification effects, and a comparison of photographs and silhouettes has been published for African American profile esthetics [1][6].

Measure how far the lips sit from the line
Identify protrusion or retrusion of lips or chin relative to the nose
Inform orthodontic, surgical or filler choices that change the profile
angle.text: The E-line is a measuring tool that turns a profile photo into numbers about lip, nose and chin balance. People use it, alone or with clinicians, to see which part of the profile is out of proportion and to preview the effect of changes before choosing a treatment.
